entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11985"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Dan.3.1-Dan.3.30">Da 3:1-30</reference>. Nebuchadnezzar's Idolatrous Image; Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego Are Delivered from the Furnace.</title> <div sID="gen21662" type="x-p"/> Between the vision of Nebuchadnezzar in the second chapter and that of Daniel in the seventh, four narratives of Daniel's and his friends' personal history are introduced. As the second and seventh chapters go together, so the third and sixth chapters (the deliverance from the lions' den), and the fourth and fifth chapters. Of these last two pairs, the former shows God's nearness to save His saints when faithful to Him, at the very time they seem to be crushed by the world power. The second pair shows, in the case of the two kings of the first monarchy, how God can suddenly humble the world power in the height of its insolence. The latter advances from mere self-glorification, in the fourth chapter, to open opposition to God in the fifth. Nebuchadnezzar demands homage to be paid to his image (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.1-Dan.3.6">Da 3:1-6</reference>), and boasts of his power (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.1-Dan.4.18">Da 4:1-18</reference>). But Belshazzar goes further, blaspheming God by polluting His holy vessels. There is a similar progression in the conduct of God's people. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego refuse positive homage to the image of the world power (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.12">Da 3:12</reference>); Daniel will not yield it even a negative homage, by omitting for a time the worship of God (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.10">Da 6:10</reference>). Jehovah's power manifested for the saints against the world in individual histories (the third through sixth chapters) is exhibited in the second and seventh chapters, in world-wide prophetical pictures; the former heightening the effect of the latter. The miracles wrought in behalf of Daniel and his friends were a manifestation of God's glory in Daniel's person, as the representative of the theocracy before the Babylonian king, who deemed himself almighty, at a time when God could not manifest it in His people as a body. They tended also to secure, by their impressive character, that respect for the covenant-people on the part of the heathen powers which issued in Cyrus' decree, not only restoring the Jews, but ascribing honor to the God of heaven, and commanding the building of the temple (<reference osisRef="Ezra.1.1-Ezra.1.4">Ezr 1:1-4</reference>) [Auberlen].<div eID="gen21662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21663" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11985"/><hi type="bold">1. image--</hi>Nebuchadnezzar's confession of God did not prevent him being a worshipper of idols, besides. Ancient idolaters thought that each nation had its own gods, and that, in addition to these, foreign gods might be worshipped. The Jewish religion was the only exclusive one that claimed all homage for Jehovah as the only true God. Men will in times of trouble confess God, if they are allowed to retain their favorite heart-idols. The image was that of Bel, the Babylonian tutelary god; or rather, Nebuchadnezzar himself, the personification and representative of the Babylonian empire, as suggested to him by the dream (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.38">Da 2:38</reference>), "Thou art this head of gold." The interval between the dream and the event here was about nineteen years. Nebuchadnezzar had just returned from finishing the Jewish and Syrian wars, the spoils of which would furnish the means of rearing such a colossal statue [Prideaux]. The colossal size makes it likely that the frame was wood, overlaid with gold. The "height," sixty cubits, is so out of proportion with the "breadth," exceeding it ten times, that it seems best to suppose the thickness from breast to back to be intended, which is exactly the right proportion of a well-formed man [Augustine, The City of God, 15.26]. Prideaux thinks the sixty cubits refer to the image and pedestal together, the image being twenty-seven cubits high, or forty feet, the pedestal thirty-three cubits, or fifty feet. Herodotus [1.183] confirms this by mentioning a similar image, forty feet high, in the temple of Belus at Babylon. It was not the same image, for the one here was on the plain of Dura, not in the city. <div eID="gen21663" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11990"/><div sID="gen21675" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11990"/>6. No other nation but the Jews would feel this edict oppressive; for it did not prevent them worshipping their own gods besides. It was evidently aimed at the Jews by those jealous of their high position in the king's court, who therefore induced the king to pass an edict as to all recusants, representing such refusal of homage as an act of treason to Nebuchadnezzar as civil and religious "head" of the empire. So the edict under Darius (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.7-Dan.6.9">Da 6:7-9</reference>) was aimed against the Jews by those jealous of Daniel's influence. The literal image of Nebuchadnezzar is a typical prophecy of "the image of the beast," connected with mystical Babylon, in <reference osisRef="Rev.13.14">Re 13:14</reference>. The second mystical beast there causeth the earth, and them that dwell therein, to worship the first beast, and that as many as would not, should be killed (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.12">Re 13:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.13.15">15</reference>).<div eID="gen21675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21676" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">furnace--</hi>a common mode of punishment in Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.22">Jr 29:22</reference>). It is not necessary to suppose that the furnace was made for the occasion. Compare "brick-kiln," <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.31">2Sa 12:31</reference>. Any furnace for common purposes in the vicinity of Dura would serve. Chardin, in his travels (A.D. 1671-1677), mentions that in Persia, to terrify those who took advantage of scarcity to sell provisions at exorbitant prices, the cooks were roasted over a slow fire, and the bakers cast into a burning oven. <div eID="gen21676" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11992"/><div sID="gen21678" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11992"/><hi type="bold">8. accused the Jews--</hi>literally, "ate the rent limbs," or flesh of the Jews (compare <reference osisRef="Job.31.31">Job 31:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.14.4">Psa 14:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.27.2">27:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.10.25">Jr 10:25</reference>). Not probably in general, but as <reference osisRef="Dan.3.12">Da 3:12</reference> states, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego. Why Daniel was not summoned does not appear. Probably he was in some distant part of the empire on state business, and the general summons (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.2">Da 3:2</reference>) had not time to reach him before the dedication. Also, the Jews' enemies found it more politic to begin by attacking Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego, who were nearer at hand, and had less influence, before they proceeded to attack Daniel. <div eID="gen21678" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12000"/><div sID="gen21686" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12000"/><hi type="bold">18. But if not, &c.--</hi>connected with <reference osisRef="Dan.3.18">Da 3:18</reference>. "Whether our God deliver us, as He is able, or do not, we will not serve thy gods." Their service of God is not mercenary in its motive. Though He slay them, they will still trust in Him (<reference osisRef="Job.13.15">Job 13:15</reference>). Their deliverance from sinful compliance was as great a miracle in the kingdom of grace, as that from the furnace was in the kingdom of nature. Their youth, and position as captives and friendless exiles, before the absolute world potentate and the horrid death awaiting them if they should persevere in their faith, all enhance the grace of God, which carried them through such an ordeal. <div eID="gen21686" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12001"/><div sID="gen21687" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12001"/><hi type="bold">19. visage ... changed--</hi>He had shown forbearance (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.14">Da 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.15">15</reference>) as a favor to them, but now that they despise even his forbearance, anger "fills" him, and is betrayed in his whole countenance.<div eID="gen21687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21688" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seven times more than it was wont--</hi>literally, "than it was (ever) seen to be heated." Passion overdoes and defeats its own end, for the hotter the fire, the sooner were they likely to be put out of pain. <div eID="gen21688" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12002"/><div sID="gen21689" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12002"/><hi type="bold">21. coats ... hosen ... hats--</hi>Herodotus [1.195] says that the Babylonian costume consisted of three parts: (1) wide, long pantaloons; (2) a woollen shirt; (3) an outer mantle with a girdle round it. So these are specified [Gesenius], "their pantaloons, inner tunics (hosen, or stockings, are not commonly worn in the East), and outer mantles." Their being cast in so hurriedly, with all their garments on, enhanced the miracle in that not even the smell of fire passed on their clothes, though of delicate, inflammable material. <div eID="gen21689" type="x-p"/>

Here follows an addition in the Septuagint, Syrian, Arabic, and Vulgate versions. "The Prayer of Azarias," and "The Song of the Three Holy Children." It is not in the Chaldee. The hymn was sung throughout the whole Church in their liturgies, from the earliest times [Rufinus in Commentary on the Apostles Creed, and Athanasius]. The "astonishment" of Nebuchadnezzar in <reference osisRef="Dan.3.24">Da 3:24</reference> is made an argument for its genuineness, as if it explained the cause of his astonishment, namely, "they walked in the midst of the fire praising God, but the angel of the Lord came down into the oven" (vs. 1 and vs. 27 of the Apocryphal addition). But <reference osisRef="Dan.3.25">Da 3:25</reference> of English Version explains his astonishment, without need of any addition. <div eID="gen21691" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12006"/><div sID="gen21693" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12006"/><hi type="bold">25. four--</hi>whereas but three had been cast in.<div eID="gen21693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21694" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">loose--</hi>whereas they had been cast in "bound." Nebuchadnezzar's question, in <reference osisRef="Dan.3.24">Da 3:24</reference>, is as if he can scarcely trust his own memory as to a fact so recent, now that he sees through an aperture in the furnace what seems to contradict it.<div eID="gen21694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21695" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">walking in ... midst of ... fire--</hi>image of the godly unhurt, and at large (<reference osisRef="John.8.36">Joh 8:36</reference>), "in the midst of trouble" (<reference osisRef="Ps.138.7">Psa 138:7</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.23.3">Psa 23:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.23.4">4</reference>). They walked up and down in the fire, not leaving it, but waiting for God's time to bring them out, just as Jesus waited in the tomb as God's prisoner, till God should let Him out (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.26">Ac 2:26</reference>, 27). So Paul (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.8">2Co 12:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.9">9</reference>). So Noah waited in the ark, after the flood, till God brought him forth (<reference osisRef="Gen.8.12-Gen.8.18">Ge 8:12-18</reference>).<div eID="gen21695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21696" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">like the Son of God--</hi>Unconsciously, like Saul, Caiaphas (<reference osisRef="John.11.49-John.11.52">Joh 11:49-52</reference>), and Pilate, he is made to utter divine truths. "Son of God" in his mouth means only an "angel" from heaven, as <reference osisRef="Dan.3.28">Da 3:28</reference> proves. Compare <reference osisRef="Job.1.6">Job 1:6</reference>; 38:7; <reference osisRef="Ps.34.7">Psa 34:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.34.8">8</reference>; and the probably heathen centurion's exclamation (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.54">Mt 27:54</reference>). The Chaldeans believed in families of gods: Bel, the supreme god, accompanied by the goddess Mylitta, being the father of the gods; thus the expression he meant: one sprung from and sent by the gods. Really it was the "messenger of the covenant," who herein gave a prelude to His incarnation. <div eID="gen21696" type="x-p"/>
